episode_title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset

stories.topic: Growing Up With 'Hum Do Hamare Do' And Realising It Was A Lie
stories.summary: Amit was taught in school that India's poverty was caused by overpopulation — the cannard of 'Hum Do Hamare Do' (We Two, Our Two). It was intuitive: poor country, too many people, not enough to go around. As he came into adulthood and looked at the actual data, he discovered the opposite was true — and he got angrier and angrier as he saw most people still believing the lie 'like sheep,' refusing to update on evidence.
stories.insight: The most insidious propaganda is the kind we absorb as children and never re-examine. Many adult convictions are just unaudited childhood programming — the antidote is the willingness to update on evidence even when it contradicts what 'everyone knows.'

stories.topic: Common-Sense Test: Why Are You In A City?
stories.summary: Amit's test for anyone who believes population density is bad: where are you right now? If you're watching from a city, why are you there — isn't density a problem? If from a village, you either earned your money in a city or want to go to one. The whole story of human history is migration from sparsely populated rural areas to dense cities — Mumbai-folk don't move to Bihar; the flow is reversed. Monaco has 40x Bangladesh's density and is far richer; Bahrain has 3x India's density and is far richer.
stories.insight: If a thing were truly bad, people would vote against it with their feet. Revealed preference — where humans actually choose to live — is a more honest signal than the loudest received wisdom about what's good for them.

stories.topic: Paul Ehrlich's Hellish Taxi Ride Through Delhi
stories.summary: Paul Ehrlich opened The Population Bomb (1968) by recounting a stinking-hot taxi ride through a Delhi slum: 'people eating, people washing, people sleeping, people visiting, arguing and screaming, people thrusting their hands through the taxi window begging, people defecating and urinating, people clinging to buses... people, people, people, people.' He confessed he had 'understood the population explosion intellectually for a long time' but came to understand it 'emotionally' that day. Amit notes Delhi in the mid-60s wasn't even that crowded — Ehrlich was clearly embellishing.
stories.insight: A 'visceral' insight that overrides data isn't an insight — it's a prejudice with adjectives. Beware the public intellectual whose argument leans on the smell of poor people rather than the numbers.

stories.topic: The Pipli Massacre — Forced Sterilisation Under The Emergency
stories.summary: In Pipli, Haryana, after a widower named Hawasingh was forcibly taken for sterilisation, his wound went septic and he bled to death. The block development officer returned demanding more 'volunteers' and forcibly grabbed a man repairing shoes by the roadside. Villagers drove the BDO out; police laid siege through the night, fired at dawn, and killed two women making cow-dung cakes outside their huts. They threatened to bomb the village by aircraft. Out of a population of 2,761, between 400 and 500 men were rounded up and sterilised.
stories.insight: When a state decides population is a 'problem,' the next step is treating people as livestock. The horror of population control isn't a bug of bad implementation — it is the logical endpoint of a state that believes it owns its citizens' bodies.

stories.topic: Sanjay Gandhi And The Quota System
stories.summary: Coomi Kapoor's reporting: there were 26.24 lakh sterilisations in 1975-76, and 81.32 lakh in 1976-77. Targets were fixed for each district; failure to meet them led to suspension, transfer, withholding of salary. Government schoolteachers were ordered to 'motivate' at least five sterilisations to receive their pay; some desperate teachers offered half their own salaries to persuade volunteers. Admission to government schools was denied to a third or fourth child; medical care, agricultural land, low-interest loans, and government jobs were tied to sterilisation certificates. In several Delhi government hospitals, treatment was denied until patients first agreed to sterilisation.
stories.insight: Targets-and-incentives bureaucracies, when applied to the human body, become engines of cruelty by design. The Emergency wasn't an aberration of family planning — it was family planning taken seriously.

stories.topic: His PhD Was On Why Malaysian Women Have Babies
stories.summary: Ajay reveals his PhD thesis was on fertility — specifically why women in Malaysia have babies. Because of that he read deep into the fertility literature, which is what lets him cite a striking pre-modern example: in interwar Poland, sandwiched between Nazi Germany and Stalin's USSR, birth rates collapsed long before modern contraception was widely available. People simply stopped having children because hope had died.
stories.insight: Fertility is a leading indicator of hope. When men and women stop having children even before contraceptives are widely available, the regime they live under has already lost the future — pessimism is a more powerful contraceptive than any pill.

stories.summary: Reflecting on the demographic dividend, Ajay recalls he learned about Bjørn Lomborg's bell-curve story of London's pollution at the turn of the 19th century — that London was once as bad as any Indian city today. The reading habit and the access to global thinkers, he says, is something his 1985-self could not have imagined. (This frames why he's so intolerant of doom narratives — he has seen, in his own lifetime, cities that 'got their shit together.')
stories.insight: Optimism, properly grounded, is empirical: the past was worse than the present, and many present horrors have already been solved somewhere. The work is to import the solutions, not to surrender to inevitability.

stories.topic: Kumar Anand's Haunting Image Of Idle Young Men In Bihar
stories.summary: Amit's friend Kumar Anand, travelling through semi-urban Bihar near Saharsa, saw streets full of young men just standing — not waiting for a bus, not at a chai katta smoking, not waiting for a contractor to pick them up. Just standing. Just idle. The image stayed with Kumar; Amit later did a Seen and Unseen episode with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand on Bihar where the same haunted observation recurred — young people who don't have jobs, or who don't even care anymore.
stories.insight: A demographic dividend without jobs is a demographic disaster. The most dangerous output of a country failing its young men isn't poverty — it's purposelessness, the corrosion of meaning that precedes political and social collapse.

stories.topic: The Bare-Branches Problem And The Dagger Wound On The Soul
stories.summary: Ajay invokes the Chinese term 'bare branches' — young men, well into their twenties, never finding their feet, never standing on their own, never building a family. He layers in another mechanism: gender-segregated upbringing in India means many young men are raised without ever talking to girls. He calls this 'a dagger wound on the soul.' Renu Sane's co-authored paper finds that as the sex ratio skews toward excess males, crime rises.
stories.insight: Gender segregation, sex-ratio imbalance, and male joblessness compound into a triad that society pays for in violence. You can't suppress the male socialisation impulse — you can only build healthy channels for it, or watch it metastasise.

stories.topic: Learning To Talk To Girls From Bollywood
stories.summary: Amit went to a boys' school. He notes wryly that he 'learned how to talk to girls by watching Bollywood, which is not quite the best thing.' This bookends the conversation about gender-segregated upbringing — even for someone from a privileged metropolitan background, the lack of natural co-ed socialisation leaves cultural fiction as the only available model.
stories.insight: When real socialisation is denied, fiction fills the vacuum — usually badly. The mass cultural products of a society teach its young what they should have learned by living, with predictable distortions in the result.

stories.topic: The Simon-Friedman Letters On Airline Overbooking
stories.summary: In December 1976, a young Julian Simon wrote to Milton Friedman proposing a sealed-bid auction for overbooked airline seats — passengers willing to take a later flight name their price. Friedman replied that the plan made obvious economic sense, but he was 'utterly baffled' that no airline had implemented it: 'I find it even harder to believe that opportunities for large increments of profit are being rejected for wholly irrational reasons.' Then Alfred Kahn — a good economist — was appointed CAB chair, the airlines tried it, and it became standard practice. Simon wrote back with an 'I told you so.' Friedman replied: 'Many thanks for your I told you so. You are entitled to it. You deserve a great deal of credit for having pushed your idea as effectively as you have.'
stories.insight: Two great men, no ego — public and gracious admission of being wrong. The willingness to say 'I was wrong, you were right, well done' is a near-extinct virtue in modern discourse, where being wrong in public has become a status injury rather than a learning event.

recommendations.item: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column setting out the case that population density drives prosperity, not poverty.
recommendations.reason: The essay version of the show's central argument: people are brains, not stomachs. Migration toward density is the dominant story of human history; every supposed 'population problem' is a governance failure in disguise.

recommendations.item: The Ultimate Resource
recommendations.creator: Julian Simon
recommendations.context: Simon's 1981 book arguing that the human mind is the ultimate resource — more people means more brains to find substitutes and innovate around scarcity.
recommendations.reason: The intellectual foundation of population-optimism. Simon's argument is that resources are functionally infinite because human ingenuity reroutes around any scarcity (fibre optics replace copper, etc.). Amit ties it to his core claim that all 'population problems' are really failures of governance.

recommendations.item: Too Many People?
recommendations.creator: Nicholas Eberstadt
recommendations.context: Eberstadt's 2007 working paper examining the empirical relationship between population density and poverty.
recommendations.reason: Cited at the top of the episode for finding no correlation between population density and poverty — and several counter-examples (Monaco's density is 40x Bangladesh's; Bahrain's is 3x India's). The data anchor for the rest of the argument.

recommendations.item: An Essay on the Principle of Population
recommendations.creator: Thomas Robert Malthus
recommendations.context: The 1798 originator of the modern pessimist tradition that population grows exponentially while resources grow arithmetically.
recommendations.reason: The seminal mistake. Amit notes Malthus actually wrote that 'instead of recommending cleanliness to the poor, we should encourage contrary habits and court the return of the plague' — because for Malthus the plague would be 'deliverance.' Read it to understand where the rot started.

recommendations.item: The Population Bomb
recommendations.creator: Paul Ehrlich
recommendations.context: The 1968 book that defined modern overpopulation panic, predicting hundreds of millions of deaths from starvation in the 1970s and 80s.
recommendations.reason: Read it to understand how spectacularly wrong elite consensus can be. Ehrlich predicted England would not exist by 2000 and that most people who would die in 'the greatest cataclysm in the history of man' were already born. He has been wrong about everything in his career and remains a hero of the left.

recommendations.item: The Book That Incited a Worldwide Fear of Overpopulation
recommendations.creator: Charles Mann
recommendations.context: Mann's Smithsonian essay revisiting The Population Bomb and the population-control movement of the 50s-70s.
recommendations.reason: Source of the chilling detail Amit reads aloud: birth-control pills literally pitched out of helicopters over Philippine villages; health workers' salaries determined by the number of IUDs they inserted. Sets the global context for what Sanjay Gandhi did in India.

recommendations.item: The Emergency: A Personal History
recommendations.creator: Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: Coomi Kapoor's account of the 1975-77 Emergency, including a chapter on Sanjay Gandhi's family-planning drive.
recommendations.reason: The single best source on the lived horror of forced sterilisation in India — quotas, salary withholding, denial of medical care without sterilisation certificates, the Pipli massacre. Amit reads multiple passages from it; one of the most important books on Indian political history.

recommendations.item: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Coomi Kapoor on the Emergency.
recommendations.reason: The companion conversation to her book, going deeper into the journalist's-eye view of how the Emergency unfolded and how it was reported (and suppressed).

recommendations.item: The Simon-Ehrlich wager
recommendations.creator: Wikipedia
recommendations.context: The Wikipedia article on the famous 1980 bet between Julian Simon and Paul Ehrlich.
recommendations.reason: The classic case study. Ehrlich picked five commodities (copper, chromium, nickel, tin, tungsten) he expected to rise in price as scarcity bit; Simon bet they'd fall as ingenuity found substitutes. Simon won — prices fell as Delhi's population quintupled. Despite this, Ehrlich remains a respected public figure.

recommendations.item: Triumph of the City
recommendations.creator: Edward Glaeser
recommendations.context: Glaeser's classic on why cities are the engines of human prosperity.
recommendations.reason: Source of Ajay's intuition that urban density is the heart of modernity — large numbers of clever people in close proximity. Modernity is an urban culture, not a rural one. Glaeser also acknowledges cities can be terrible (NYC in the 70s) — but they are learnable problems, not natural disasters.

recommendations.item: The Skeptical Environmentalist
recommendations.creator: Bjørn Lomborg
recommendations.context: Lomborg's data-driven challenge to environmentalist doom narratives.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's bell-curve framing for cities — London at the turn of the 19th century was as polluted as any Indian city today. Cities arc through pollution and dysfunction toward livability if humans act purposively. (Ajay cautions: there is no inevitability — it requires purposive human action.)

recommendations.item: The Origins of Totalitarianism
recommendations.creator: Hannah Arendt
recommendations.context: Arendt's seminal work on the structural similarities between Nazi Germany and Stalin's Russia.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's primary recommendation. Arendt mapped the deep family resemblance between national-socialist and communist totalitarianism — and her argument that totalitarian regimes 'run out of people to oppress' is the lens through which Ajay reads the population busts of Putin's Russia and post-one-child China. Amit adds: it is a book of the present, not history.

recommendations.item: Yuganta
recommendations.creator: Irawati Karve
recommendations.context: Karve's 1936 critical examination of the Mahabharata and the role of women within it.
recommendations.reason: Amit's primary recommendation. A masterpiece of literary criticism that doubles as an analysis of contemporary Indian society — what Karve writes about the epics is, distressingly, still about us. Like Arendt's book, it isn't a book of another time and space; it's about this age.

recommendations.item: What Bruce Springsteen Means to Us (Episode 13, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier EIE episode on Springsteen.
recommendations.reason: Cited as the source of Ajay's invocation of two Springsteen lines about a child being 'another shot' — that having a child is 'a moment of optimism, the tendrils of optimism creeping out of your heart.'

recommendations.item: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier EIE episode on the Ukraine war.
recommendations.reason: Background for Ajay's claim that ~300,000 reproductive-age Russian men have died in Ukraine and roughly a million have left, reshaping Russian demographics for generations.

recommendations.item: Understanding Baumol's Cost Disease And Its Impact On Healthcare
recommendations.creator: Varun Ganapathi
recommendations.context: An essay introducing Baumol's cost-disease — why services like haircuts and string-quartet performances get more expensive even as manufacturing gets cheaper.
recommendations.reason: Ajay refuses to be sidetracked into explaining it himself: 'Just leaving things, lovely things for people to Google.' The concept matters because in an aging society where many old people need young-person services (nursing, cooking, cleaning), Baumol's effect makes these services prohibitively expensive.

recommendations.item: The Evil of Family Planning
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2014 column responding to deaths in a Chhattisgarh sterilisation camp.
recommendations.reason: His earlier polemic against the institutional cruelty of state-driven family planning — written after a botched mass-sterilisation drive killed several women, with contaminated instruments and broken autoclaves as 'garden-variety incompetence of the Indian state.'

recommendations.item: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (Episode 345, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand
recommendations.context: A road-trip episode through Bihar.
recommendations.reason: The full conversation behind Kumar Anand's haunting image of streets full of idle young men in semi-urban Bihar — the human face of demographic dividend turning into demographic disaster.

recommendations.item: The Effect of Age-Specific Sex Ratios on Crime: Instrumental Variable Estimates from India
recommendations.creator: Rashmi Barua, Prarthna Goel and Renuka Sane
recommendations.context: An empirical paper on the relationship between sex ratios and crime in India.
recommendations.reason: Cited for the finding that as sex ratios skew toward excess males, crime rises — the data anchor for Ajay's bare-branches argument and the 'dagger wound on the soul' of male gender segregation.

recommendations.item: The Great Breakthrough and Its Cause
recommendations.creator: Julian Simon
recommendations.context: Simon's last book, edited and finished by Timur Kuran (Ajay's old teacher).
recommendations.reason: Expounds Simon's earlier thesis that the industrial revolution and productivity booms happened because populations went up — multiplying the number of games, allowing voluntary exchange, and benefitting everyone. The deeper version of 'people are brains, not stomachs.'

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on the principles of good economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show's standing resources; relevant here for Ajay's framing of state coercion having no natural budget constraint — unlike spending, which is checked by tax extraction, coercive interventions can scale up unchecked unless citizens push back.

core_ideas.explanation: The central thesis. Malthusians see a person as a mouth to feed — pure liability. The economic view sees a person as a brain and pair of hands — net producer over a lifetime. More people therefore means more wealth, not less. Anyone who calls population a problem is implicitly saying that other people are the problem: 'I am not, I am above all of this.' That moral exclusion is the tell.

Cities are great because of urban density — large numbers of clever people within twenty minutes of each other. Each of us is the creature of the people who surround us. If an evil government dispersed everyone on a hundred-metre grid, the agglomeration would die and modernity with it. Modernity is not a rural culture, not the culture of landowners and toxic masculinity — it is created in dense human collections. (Ajay caveats: bad cities are possible, but the difficulties of urbanism are learnable problems.)

core_ideas.concept: Induced Innovation And The Price System
core_ideas.explanation: When a resource grows scarce, the price system raises a flag and humans innovate around it — fibre optics displacing copper, petroleum displacing whale oil. Linear extrapolation of trends is the cardinal Malthusian error. Julian Simon's joke: extrapolate the recent expansion of university buildings forward and one day the entire planet would be university buildings. Common sense — and price signals — never let that happen.

core_ideas.concept: Why Poor People Have More Children
core_ideas.explanation: Two interlocking reasons: (1) children are an economic asset and old-age insurance — viable producers, not just dependents; (2) historically high childhood mortality made having more an actuarial necessity. As childhood mortality declines, fertility lags; the rich consequently have fewer children. Far from being irrational reproduction, high fertility among the poor is rational risk management given their conditions.

core_ideas.concept: The Coercion Spectrum (Pre-Emergency vs. Emergency vs. China)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's three-point comparison of family-planning regimes: pre-Emergency India (modest state coercion), Emergency India (terrifying — power concentrated in Sanjay Gandhi, no one with the guts to tell the dictator he was full of it), and Mao's China (the one-child policy, draconian beyond belief). The lesson: power concentrated in one or two people lets terrible ideas become accepted because dissent disappears. Family planning is a case study in the importance of dispersed power.
core_ideas.quote: When power gets concentrated in one or two people, many terrible ideas become accepted because nobody has the guts to tell the dictator that you know you're full of it.

core_ideas.concept: The Body Is The Last Frontier Of Coercion
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing: there is a spectrum of state intrusion. A government telling a Punjab farmer not to burn his fields is one level; a government telling a single woman she cannot use surrogacy is a totally different level of evil — because it interferes with her body and personal life. The further the state moves from public goods toward the body, the more illegitimate the coercion. 'All questions connected to having children should be the bloody business of individuals.'

When governments spend money there is a natural check — tax extraction is hard, citizens rebel and hide wealth, so spending is rate-limited. But coercion has no analogous brake. Governments can pile coercion on coercion with no budget. There are no fine sensibilities about degrees of coercion. Citizens must therefore rebel far more aggressively against intrusive coercion — because nothing else will stop it.
core_ideas.quote: There's no budget constraint in coercion.

core_ideas.concept: Totalitarians Run Out Of People To Oppress
core_ideas.explanation: Hannah Arendt's lesson, applied. Authoritarian regimes create hopelessness, economic and cultural stagnation, and a culture of coercion. Men and women respond by going on strike — they stop having children. Putin's Russia, Stalin's Russia, Mao's China, Nazi Germany — all of them suffer severe depopulation. The ~300,000 reproductive-age Russian men killed in Ukraine plus the ~1 million best-and-brightest who fled = ~1.3 million-person hole in Russia's demographic future, much of it before any contraception decision is made.

core_ideas.concept: Having A Child Is An Act Of Hope
core_ideas.explanation: Fertility is a primal vote on the future. Inter-war Poland — wedged between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union — saw birth rates collapse before modern contraception was widespread. People simply stopped having children. Choosing to have a child requires a settled inner happiness and an external sense that the world will be safe enough, prosperous enough, free enough. Authoritarian governments make those conditions impossible.
core_ideas.quote: When hope dies, you stop having children.

core_ideas.explanation: Far from a population bomb, the modern threat is a population bust. Western countries (US, UK) had a long, slow fertility decline — society had generations to adjust. Russia and China experienced abrupt collapses, leaving wrenching age structures. India is now showing rapid fertility decline as well, and the absence of a 2021 census means we don't even have good data. The mechanism: rational individuals respond to bad jobs, cramped housing, long commutes, gender imbalance, and a fearful state by not having kids.

core_ideas.concept: Baumol's Cost Disease And The Aging-Society Trap
core_ideas.explanation: In an aging society, the elderly need services that can only be produced by younger people — nursing, cooking, cleaning, personal care. Push pension wealth aside and look at pure arithmetic: if 10% of society is old they can be served by 15% young; if 40% is old, 60% young is not feasible because other things must be produced too. Non-tradeable services hit an exchange-rate problem — prices go to infinity, and old age loses its dignity. This is the second-order economic consequence of fertility collapse.

The Chinese term for young men who fail to find their feet — no trade, no income, no independent household, no family. Combined with sex-ratio imbalance and gender-segregated upbringing in India, the result is what Ajay calls 'a dagger wound on the soul.' Empirically, sex ratios skewed toward excess males correlate with higher crime (Barua-Goel-Sane). Neuroscience adds a layer: the male socialisation centre of the brain doesn't fully develop until ~25, which is why most violence in the world is by 18-25-year-old males. Add scarcity of female partners and you get the demographic preconditions of a deeply unstable society.

Ajay's aside on Indian statistics. The last official census was in 2011 — a 2021 one never happened, 'as far as we can tell, there's no census going on around us.' Even when it did happen, census data was always messy: there's a 'Indian-style gerrymandering' literature on how the census itself was manipulated to draw electoral maps. Together with the GDP, the IIP, the NSSO and the ASI all measuring poorly, India runs blind on the most basic indicators. Alternative sources still suggest a rapid fertility decline.

Ajay's prescription. India's social and legal architecture privileges the two-parent heteronormative family for raising children — which excludes single parents, same-sex couples, and other arrangements that many people would gladly choose. Loosening these rules would simultaneously: (a) reflect the blossoming of human freedom, and (b) be practically necessary in a society where total fertility is collapsing. More eclectic, unconventional ways for people to have and raise children should be welcomed.

The exchange between Milton Friedman and Julian Simon over airline overbooking is held up as a vanished ideal of intellectual discourse. Friedman, a giant, wrote to a young Simon initially saying the plan was good but couldn't be right because someone would already have done it. Years later when Simon proved correct, Friedman wrote: 'Many thanks for your I told you so, you are entitled to it. You deserve a great deal of credit for having pushed your idea as effectively as you have.' No ego, no face-saving, just truth-tracking. In the current social-media environment, where being wrong in public is treated as a status injury, this model is increasingly extinct.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: On state-imposed sterilisation always falling on women: 'It's not like one man is not gonna go up to another man and slap him on the back and say bhai, that never happens. It is always specifically the women who suffer.'

Amit on the source of the 'maggots on a dead cow' chapter title — a real quote from Harrison Brown, who wrote that humanity 'will not rest content until the earth is covered completely and to a considerable depth with a writhing mass of human beings, much as a dead cow is covered with a pulsating mass of maggots.' He was 'all for forcible sterilization and eugenics.'

Julian Simon's joke about linear extrapolation: take the recent rate at which university buildings have expanded, project it forward, and 'one day there would be nothing on the earth except university buildings.'
Amit, after a heavy chapter on the Emergency, gestures to the cat in the studio: 'Even the beautiful kitten behind us agrees with me, we are partners in this pie.'
Ajay deflecting the Baumol's-cost-disease tangent: 'I don't want to get sidetracked into that. Just leaving things, lovely things for people to Google. Please go study Baumol's cost disease.'
Amit on his own sex education: 'I went to a boys' school. I learned how to talk to girls by watching Bollywood, which is not quite the best thing.'
Amit's mock-provocation: 'I sometimes provocatively say that most Urdu poetry is a whining of incels. But you know that's just a provocation — but the whining of incels could become a problem.'
Ajay on Indian government-camp sterilisations going wrong: contaminated instruments, broken autoclaves — 'that's garden-variety incompetence of the Indian state. That's unsurprising.'
Amit on Ehrlich's grand prediction record: 'He has been wrong about everything in his life. Anyway...'
'Hum Do Hamare Do' — the post-Independence Indian government's slogan urging couples to have only two children, the soundtrack of decades of state-driven family planning.

Pipli, Haryana — village 45 km north of Delhi where, during the Emergency, police laid siege overnight, threatened to bomb the village, and forcibly sterilised 400-500 men out of a population of 2,761. Two women making cow-dung cakes outside their huts were shot dead at dawn.

Bansi Lal of Haryana — 'most notoriously' the chief minister who bent over backwards to please Sanjay Gandhi during the Emergency, with Haryana achieving four times its sterilisation target in 1976-77.
Nasbandi (the Hindi word for vasectomy) — the cultural shadow-word of the Emergency, still freighted with memories of forced sterilisation.

'I have understood the population explosion intellectually for a long time. I came to understand it emotionally one stinking hot day in Delhi a few years ago...' — Paul Ehrlich's notorious opening passage, weaponised here as the tell of a man whose 'data' was actually disgust.

Alfred E. Kahn — the economist appointed CAB chair in the late 1970s, whose appointment finally allowed Julian Simon's airline-overbooking-auction idea to be implemented (a 'good economist, because not all economists get economics, but he gets it').

'Bare branches' — Chinese term for unmarried young men with no descendants, used by Ajay to describe the social problem of male joblessness, gender imbalance, and the resulting moral catastrophe in young men's lives.

The Treaty of Versailles birthing inter-war Poland — sandwiched between Hitler's Germany and Stalin's USSR, with Trotsky stopped at its eastern edge. Used as a fertility case study: people stopped having children before any modern contraception was available.

Robert Sapolsky on Sam Harris's podcast — Amit's source for the neuroscience claim that the male socialisation centre of the brain doesn't fully develop until 25, which explains why most violence is committed by males aged 18-25.

Bruce Springsteen on having children — Ajay paraphrases two Springsteen lines (from EIE Episode 13) on the act of having a child: 'another shot... a moment of optimism, the tendrils of optimism creeping out of your heart.'
